---
title: "Plugin developer SDK"
---

The SDK gives you a small starting point for developing a BenchWeave device plugin with AI: **generate → implement → test → review → prepare a release**. Use this guide for SDK installation, project generation, testing and packaging. The [device developer guide](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/device-developer-guide.md) (main repository) covers device evidence, integration requirements, firmware and qualification.

The device is the hardware; the plugin is its Python integration and descriptor. Follow the [developer directory convention](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/device-developer-guide.md#repository-layout-for-device-plugins): `plugins/<manufacturer>/<name>/`, with `src/<python_package>/` inside that project. The name normally identifies the device model, such as `fnirsi/dps150`.

The current SDK is `benchweave-sdk` 0.1.0 for Python 3.13+, OTDP 0.2.1 and adapter API 1.1, with registry 0.1.1 schemas. Its source lives in this repository, mounted at `packages/sdk` in the [main BenchWeave repository](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave), and is built separately from the gateway. It supplies structural typing interfaces, offline contract validation, a scripted mock host, bounded async conformance helpers, an external project generator and file-inventory helpers.

## 1. Install the SDK and generate your project

Install the SDK from PyPI:

```sh
pip install benchweave-sdk
# or as an isolated CLI tool
uv tool install benchweave-sdk
```

For bleeding-edge work before a release, install straight from the default branch:

```sh
pip install git+https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave-sdk.git
```

Full channel list: see the README Installation section.

PyPI is the default install channel: `pip install benchweave-sdk` or `uv pip install benchweave-sdk`. Contributors and maintainers can instead build from a checkout of the main BenchWeave repository — run this from that checkout's root; `packages/sdk` is the submodule mount path there, not a directory in this repository:

```sh
uv build packages/sdk --out-dir dist/sdk
```

In your development directory, create an environment and install the built wheel from the checkout's `dist/sdk/`:

```sh
uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install dist/sdk/benchweave_sdk-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
benchweave-sdk new plugins/acme/model100 --package benchweave_acme_model100
cd plugins/acme/model100
uv pip install -e '.[test]'
pytest
```

Keep using the environment containing the SDK wheel; if you create a new environment inside the project, install the wheel there too. For a repeatable `uv lock` against a locally built wheel, configure that wheel or your organisation's package source explicitly.

Replace `acme/model100` with your manufacturer and device/plugin name. The destination controls the directory hierarchy; `--package` controls the Python import package. The SDK creates missing parent directories and refuses to overwrite an existing project. A destination reached through a symlinked directory (for example `/tmp/...` on macOS) is canonicalized before any write, and messages report the real path.

```text
plugins/
└── acme/
    └── model100/                       # Independent build/test/release root
        ├── pyproject.toml
        ├── README.md
        ├── AI-GUIDE.md
        ├── CLAUDE.md                   # Agent notes; root dev tooling
        ├── src/benchweave_acme_model100/
        │   ├── __init__.py
        │   ├── adapter.py
        │   ├── protocol.py
        │   ├── descriptor.json
        │   ├── protocol.md
        │   ├── vectors.json
        │   └── skills/                 # Seeded agent skills; ship in the wheel
        │       ├── develop-plugin/SKILL.md
        │       └── drive-device/SKILL.md
        └── tests/test_plugin.py
```

Generate and retain the dependency lock, add your chosen licence file, and add `firmware/` with its own build/tests when developing custom firmware. These project-specific files are not invented by the starter. The manufacturer/name directory can be copied into its own external repository unchanged; it has no runtime dependency on BenchWeave core or the SDK. The SDK is a development dependency.

The starter deliberately implements a made-up, read-only identify/voltage protocol. Passing its tests demonstrates that the tools work; it says nothing about your instrument.

## 2. Give the AI the facts and prompts

Open the generated **`AI-GUIDE.md`**. It contains five copyable prompts: establish device facts, implement with mocks, demonstrate behaviour, prepare independent review, and prepare release artefacts for owner review.

Provide the exact model, firmware, transport, supported operations and authoritative protocol evidence. Review the AI's proposed scope before replacing the example. It should keep protocol parsing separate from the async adapter and use only supplied scoped host services. The current gateway loader supports package-relative and standard-library imports; arbitrary third-party runtime dependencies need additional integration work.

For custom hardware, follow [Build my own device firmware](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/develop-your-device.md) (main repository) as well. Firmware and the Python plugin have separate builds and compatibility evidence, even when maintained in one project.

## 3. Run the checks

From your plugin project, using the environment containing the SDK:

```sh
pytest
benchweave-sdk check src/benchweave_acme_model100/descriptor.json
uv build
```

Generated tests cover identify/read, quiet lifecycle, invalid inputs, pre-dispatch cancellation/expiry and uncertain malformed/transport responses. Extend them for your actual operations, failure modes and evidence. `check_operation` validates request/result schemas and correlation. `check_lifecycle` checks a quiet lifecycle and repeated cleanup. Both bound cooperative async calls with a configurable wall-clock timeout; blocking Python or code that suppresses cancellation needs process-level isolation.

Descriptor checks currently cover its schema, matching capabilities/policies, unique parameter names, ordered ranges and transport-provider declarations (next subsection). These are **partial checks**, not all S01–S18, C01–C12 or M01–M14 obligations. The SDK provides no physical transport provider, complete profile/capture test harness or hardware qualification certificate.

### Transport providers (custom transports) {#transport-providers}

A `custom` transport may declare a pinned **transport-provider contract** (OTDP 0.2.1): an optional `provider` object on the transport carrying the required `feature_id` and an `{id, path, sha256}` pin to the reviewed contract document inside your plugin package. `benchweave-sdk check` verifies the whole declaration offline and refuses with named, machine-matchable prefixes:

- `provider_feature_missing:` — the provider's `feature_id` is not in `required_features`.
- `provider_transport_undeclared:` — an `otdp.transport.*` feature is required but no provider on the custom transport declares it, or the provider's `feature_id` is not a sanctioned `otdp.transport.<name>/<semver>` id (a declaration nothing admissible can ever back).
- `unknown_otdp_feature:` — an `otdp.*` feature id that is neither corpus-known nor declared through a provider; the namespace is corpus-owned, and a typo or a fake version does not pass.
- `provider_contract_missing:` — the pin does not resolve to a contained regular file. Provider pins are **descriptor-relative** (the contract ships beside your descriptor, subdirectories allowed) and refuse traversal, absolute paths and symlinked components.
- `provider_contract_hash_mismatch:` — the pinned bytes do not hash to the pinned `sha256`.
- `provider_contract_invalid:` — the pinned document fails the transport-provider contract schema, its grammar subschemas are not valid Draft 2020-12 schemas, its kinds are not unique strings, a kind shadows a generic transfer kind, or its identity fields disagree — including disagreeing with the descriptor's own declaration.

A misplaced provider (on a non-custom transport, or without the adapter integration mode) and provider-object shape faults refuse through the ordinary schema-validation error surface. A `custom` transport **without** a provider stays valid: that is the honestly-incomplete posture, not a refusal. The Python entry points behind these checks are `validation.validate_transport_provider` (contract documents) and `validation.verify_provider_pin` (pin resolution).

These checks prove the declaration **well-formed and self-consistent** only. Only the gateway can prove the grant: that your host has admitted the pinned contract and that `connection_key` resolves to a connection it backs. An offline pass is not an admission claim.

## Local UI preview (simulated)

[`benchweave-sdk check-ui`](../reference/cli/check_ui.qmd), [`check-preset`](../reference/cli/check_preset.qmd) and [`preview-ui`](../reference/cli/preview_ui.qmd) validate presentation candidates and preview them offline. `preview-ui` serves the versioned preview API and the bundled React renderer on loopback only; every scenario, observation and control receipt is simulated and labelled as such — the preview path has no gateway, registry or hardware reach. An external development renderer (`--renderer-url`, e.g. a local Vite dev server) must also name a loopback host; non-loopback renderer origins are rejected because plugin authors can suggest command lines. The served document's shape is pinned by [plugin-ui-preview-v1](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/standards/plugin-ui-preview-v1/preview-document.schema.json) (main repository), validated from both the Python emitter and the renderer's decoder. Previews render the manifest's declared plots and channel hints from per-scenario snapshot values — one simulated value per observed target, not observation history.

The SDK's runtime dependencies are Click, jsonschema (+ referencing, rfc3339-validator, rfc3987 format backends), Rich and Textual — all declared in this repository's `pyproject.toml` (the file at `packages/sdk/pyproject.toml` in a main-checkout layout); the wheel vendors the canonical contract JSONs, the pure presentation validator and the built renderer assets.

Operational notes: `preview-ui` is an interactive tool — with output redirected (or `--no-open`) it serves until interrupted by design, exiting 0 on SIGINT as a normal stop; a fixed `--port` can hit a short `EADDRINUSE` window on immediate restart (deliberate anti-port-steal posture — prefer the default ephemeral port); request bodies have no handler timeout, which only matters for untrusted peers under the explicitly acknowledged `--allow-network` mode.

## Capture without a gateway (standalone writer)

Plugin and bench development happens on machines that never run the gateway. `benchweave_sdk.capture.StandaloneCaptureWriter` implements the three capture methods an adapter calls in gateway mode — `artifact_append`, `artifact_finalise`, `artifact_abort` — over one directory per capture on a local filesystem. It is three of the eight `CaptureServices` members: device I/O still comes from a transport a composing runtime supplies.

```python
from benchweave_sdk.capture import StandaloneCaptureWriter

writer = StandaloneCaptureWriter()          # or StandaloneCaptureWriter(some_path)
await writer.artifact_append("cap-demo-1", chunk, context)
manifest = await writer.artifact_finalise("cap-demo-1", {
    "format": "waveform_f64le",
    "started_at": "2026-09-22T00:00:00Z",
    "sample_count": 1024, "sample_interval_s": 0.001, "unit": "V",
}, context)
```

The capture root is an explicit constructor argument, then the `BENCHWEAVE_CAPTURE_DIR` environment variable, then `captures/` under the current working directory; a root inside the installed package tree is refused (a reinstall or upgrade wipes it, and the SDK's inventory verification refuses unlisted files). Each capture event is one directory — `manifest.json`, a `staging/` tree while chunks accumulate, the primary artifact (`<capture_id>.f64` for `waveform_f64le`, `.bin` for `raw_binary`, `.csv`/`.txt`/`.vcd` for declared extension formats, `.data` otherwise) and an optional `renderings/` tree the plugin writes itself. The manifest's `sha256`, `byte_length` and `artifact_id` (`art-<sha256>`) are computed over the real published bytes, and standalone extras live under `x-standalone-*` keys. The finalise format must be in the constructor's declared set (`formats=`, the two core formats by default; an empty set refuses everything); a capture that appended nothing is refused rather than published empty; an abort deletes only `staging/` and the in-flight primary, so a published capture and `renderings/` survive an unconditional `finally`-cleanup abort. There is no automatic import of standalone captures into the gateway — ingest is a separate, deliberate path.

### A standalone runtime around the writer (worked example)

The writer is three of the eight members. A bench script that drives an adapter without a gateway needs the other five as well: clocks, evidence, and the transport. The example below is one complete `CaptureServices` object for a device on a serial port, adapted from the serial host a contributor fork of the ADC board wrote for the same purpose. It implements the three scoped stream transactions of OTDP §8.1 exactly, plus one behaviour the spec leaves unspecified — the quiet-line answer below: `stream_send`, `stream_receive` and `stream_exchange`, with `exact_bytes` taking precedence over `termination`, `lf`/`crlf` only (serial has no `eom`), unspecified fields refused, and an incomplete frame never returned as complete. A receive that sees no bytes at all for a short quiet window answers `{"data": b""}`: nothing was offered, which adapters read as a quiet line (the DPS-150 plugin's telemetry drain ends on exactly that) rather than as an error. Once a frame has started it is only ever returned whole, and bytes already read when a deadline expires stay buffered for the next receive, so a slow reply is not lost. The capture methods delegate to `StandaloneCaptureWriter`. This is author-side tooling, not an SDK module: copy it into your project and adapt it.

```python
import asyncio
import json
import time
from datetime import UTC, datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from benchweave_sdk.capture import StandaloneCaptureWriter

_TERMINATORS = {"lf": b"\n", "crlf": b"\r\n"}
_RECEIVE = {"max_bytes", "termination", "exact_bytes"}
_FIELDS = {
    "stream_send": {"kind", "data"},
    "stream_receive": {"kind"} | _RECEIVE,
    "stream_exchange": {"kind", "data"} | _RECEIVE,
}


class BenchContext:
    """A minimal OperationContext for bench use: identity, deadline, cancellation."""

    def __init__(self, operation_id: str, timeout_s: float,
                 dataset_id: str | None = None) -> None:
        self.operation_id = operation_id
        self.dataset_id = dataset_id
        self.deadline_monotonic = time.monotonic() + timeout_s
        self.dispatched = False
        self._cancelled = False

    def cancel(self) -> None:
        self._cancelled = True

    def is_cancelled(self) -> bool:
        return self._cancelled

    async def mark_dispatch_started(self) -> None:
        self.dispatched = True


class SerialStandaloneHost:
    """All eight CaptureServices members over one serial port, without a gateway.

    ``port`` is anything with pyserial's ``write(bytes)``, ``read(size) -> bytes``
    (returning early on the port's own short timeout, which bounds how quickly a
    deadline or cancellation is noticed) and ``close()``. ``quiet_s`` is how long
    a receive waits for its first byte before answering that nothing was offered.
    """

    def __init__(self, port: Any, *, writer: Any = None, evidence_path: Path | None = None,
                 max_frame_bytes: int = 4096, quiet_s: float = 0.1) -> None:
        self._port = port
        self._writer = writer if writer is not None else StandaloneCaptureWriter()
        self._evidence_path = evidence_path
        self._max_frame = max_frame_bytes
        self._quiet_s = quiet_s
        self._pending = bytearray()  # read from the port, not yet returned
        self._closed = False
        self.evidence: list[dict[str, Any]] = []

    # clocks
    def monotonic(self) -> float:
        return time.monotonic()

    def utc_now(self) -> str:
        return datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(timespec="milliseconds").replace("+00:00", "Z")

    # transport (OTDP section 8.1 stream transactions)
    def _live(self, context: Any) -> None:
        if context.is_cancelled() or self.monotonic() >= context.deadline_monotonic:
            raise TimeoutError("operation cancelled or expired")
        if self._closed:
            raise ConnectionError("serial port is closed")

    async def transfer(self, transaction: dict[str, Any], context: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
        kind = transaction.get("kind")
        if kind not in _FIELDS or set(transaction) != _FIELDS[kind]:
            raise ValueError(f"not a section 8.1 stream transaction: {sorted(transaction)}")
        receive = None
        if kind != "stream_send":
            receive = self._receive_bounds(transaction)
        if kind != "stream_receive" and not isinstance(transaction["data"], bytes):
            raise ValueError("data must be bytes")
        self._live(context)
        if kind != "stream_receive":
            data = transaction["data"]
            try:
                sent = await asyncio.to_thread(self._port.write, data)
            except OSError as error:
                raise ConnectionError(f"serial write failed: {error}") from error
            # pyserial reports a short count without raising when a pending write
            # is cancelled, or under write_timeout=0. None means the port reports
            # no count (pyserial's own rs485.RS485 and cp2110:// ports).
            if sent is not None and sent != len(data):
                raise ConnectionError(f"serial write reported {sent} of {len(data)} bytes")
            if kind == "stream_send":
                return {}
        return {"data": await self._receive(*receive, context)}

    def _receive_bounds(self, t: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[int, bytes, int]:
        max_bytes, termination, exact = t["max_bytes"], t["termination"], t["exact_bytes"]
        if not isinstance(max_bytes, int) or isinstance(max_bytes, bool) \
                or not 1 <= max_bytes <= self._max_frame:
            raise ValueError(f"max_bytes must be 1..{self._max_frame}")
        if termination not in _TERMINATORS:  # serial does not support "eom"
            raise ValueError("termination must be 'lf' or 'crlf' on a serial port")
        if exact is not None and (not isinstance(exact, int) or isinstance(exact, bool)
                                  or not 0 <= exact <= max_bytes):
            raise ValueError("exact_bytes must be None or 0..max_bytes")
        return max_bytes, _TERMINATORS[termination], exact or 0

    async def _receive(self, max_bytes: int, terminator: bytes, exact: int, context: Any) -> bytes:
        quiet_until = self.monotonic() + self._quiet_s
        while True:
            if exact:  # a positive exact_bytes takes precedence over termination
                if len(self._pending) >= exact:
                    return self._take(exact)
            else:
                end = self._pending[:max_bytes].find(terminator)
                if end >= 0:
                    return self._take(end + len(terminator))
                if len(self._pending) >= max_bytes:
                    self._take(max_bytes)  # discard, so the next call can resynchronise
                    raise ValueError(f"no terminator within {max_bytes} bytes")
            if not self._pending and self.monotonic() >= quiet_until:
                return b""  # nothing offered: a quiet line, not an error
            self._live(context)  # a partial frame stays pending across the timeout
            want = (exact or max_bytes) - len(self._pending)
            try:
                chunk = await asyncio.to_thread(self._port.read, max(1, want))
            except OSError as error:
                raise ConnectionError(f"serial read failed: {error}") from error
            self._pending += chunk

    def _take(self, count: int) -> bytes:
        out = bytes(self._pending[:count])
        del self._pending[:count]
        return out

    async def close_transport(self, context: Any) -> None:
        if not self._closed:
            self._closed = True
            await asyncio.to_thread(self._port.close)

    # evidence
    async def record_evidence(self, entry: dict[str, Any], context: Any) -> None:
        record = {**entry, "at": self.utc_now(), "operation_id": context.operation_id}
        self.evidence.append(record)
        if self._evidence_path is not None:
            with self._evidence_path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as stream:
                stream.write(json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True) + "\n")

    # capture: the SDK's standalone writer
    async def artifact_append(self, capture_id: str, data: bytes, context: Any) -> None:
        await self._writer.artifact_append(capture_id, data, context)

    async def artifact_finalise(self, capture_id: str, metadata: dict[str, Any],
                                context: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return await self._writer.artifact_finalise(capture_id, metadata, context)

    async def artifact_abort(self, capture_id: str) -> None:
        await self._writer.artifact_abort(capture_id)
```

Using it with pyserial and a plugin's adapter:

```python
import serial  # pyserial, installed separately

port = serial.Serial("/dev/ttyUSB0", 115200, timeout=0.05)
host = SerialStandaloneHost(port, writer=StandaloneCaptureWriter(formats=("raw_binary",)))
plugin = create_plugin()
open_context = BenchContext("open", timeout_s=2.0)
await plugin.open(descriptor, host, open_context)
op_context = BenchContext("bench-1", timeout_s=2.0)
result = await plugin.execute({"operation_id": "bench-1", "verb": "read",
                               "arguments": {"parameter": "voltage"}}, op_context)
```

Give each operation its own `BenchContext`; the adapter checks `operation_id` against the request. `tests/test_guide_serial_host.py` executes the first block above and drives a freshly scaffolded plugin through it, so the example cannot drift from the SDK or from the generated adapter.

## 4. Review compatibility and deployment

Use the [AI device integration reviewer](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/ai-device-reviewer.md) (main repository) with the exact revision and test evidence. Its SDK maintenance checklist covers public interfaces, contracts, generated projects, mocks, gateway compatibility and release artefacts.

The gateway now has an explicit `load_otdp_plugin`/`OTDPBridge` path for async adapter API 1.1. Its supported host operations are **identify, scalar read, scalar write and single-channel capture** — the `capture` verb with pre-dispatch bounds checks, staged appends and a host-computed manifest (the step's `timeout_ms` is the capture budget). The release smoke exercises a generated multi-module plugin through identify/read; separate bridge tests cover write conversion and rejection paths. Profile actions and streaming remain unsupported by this bridge. The existing simulator loader is retained for its separate synchronous interface.

A gateway integrator must first complete admission, supply the verified manifest/cache and descriptor, inject authorised scoped services, and use the same monotonic timebase as the host's deadlines. The loader rechecks all listed file hashes and imports verified package code/resources in memory. This is integrity checking and namespace isolation, not an operating-system sandbox. Adapters remain trusted Python.

An SDK install does **not** add a plugin to a running workbench. There is no live device-install endpoint, automatic dependency installer or Docker hot-install command. A Docker deployment still needs persistent verified package storage, bench configuration, commissioned host services and activation at an approved idle boundary. See [package formats and gateway installation](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/develop-your-device.md#package-format-and-gateway-installation) (main repository).

## 5. Prepare the release, then approve publication

A Python wheel/source distribution and a registry release are different artefacts. Prepare the registry-required identity, exact compatibility, payload inventory, hashes, dependency locks, licence, source/build provenance, SBOM and evidence status. [`benchweave-sdk inventory <prepared-bundle-directory>`](../reference/cli/inventory.qmd) prints file paths, byte counts and SHA-256 values; it does not create or approve a complete registry manifest.

Show the owner the actual built files, evidence and remaining gaps before publishing. Hardware qualification and local commissioning remain separate. The SDK retains the project's proprietary licence declaration; release owners must establish distribution rights before sharing it publicly.

## Maintenance and release cycle

The main repository's Package workflow builds the gateway and SDK from source distributions, then tests installed wheels in temporary environments on Linux and macOS. It generates, builds and installs an external plugin outside the checkout, runs its tests, checks packaged contract bytes and versions, exercises gateway loading and rejects tampered code.

Run the same check locally from a checkout of the main BenchWeave repository (`scripts/sdk_smoke.py` lives there, not in this repository):

```sh
uv run --no-project --python 3.13 scripts/sdk_smoke.py --out-dir dist/packages
```

On a published GitHub release, a separate job repeats these checks before attaching the SDK wheel and source distribution to that release. Tagging a release triggers the publish workflow, which builds the sdist and wheel, smoke-installs the wheel on five OS/arch lanes (Linux x86-64 and arm64, macOS arm64 and Intel, and Windows), verifies each installed wheel's vendored standards with `benchweave-sdk sync-standards --check`, and publishes to PyPI via Trusted Publishing. No release is published simply by editing these files or running the local smoke check.

An installed SDK can verify its own vendored standards offline: `benchweave-sdk sync-standards --check` compares the packaged lock with the packaged tree and needs no repository checkout. Importing a standards bundle rewrites the source tree, so it is refused outside a checkout (`sync_requires_repo_checkout:`).

When changing the SDK API, canonical contracts, template, gateway bridge or build tooling, update the affected tests and documentation together. Keep SDK distribution metadata, `__version__`, generated development dependency and this compatibility statement aligned; the smoke checks guard the installed distribution and contract resources.
